original_question: A nonempty class X of finite groups is said to be complete if X is closed under taking subgroups, homomorphic images, and extensions. The symmetric boundary of a complete class X other than the class of all finite groups is defined as the largest integer n such that Sn ∈ X. Every positive integer n ̸= 3 coincides with the symmetric boundary of some complete class. It is proved(mod CFSG, D. O. Revin, Algebra i Analiz, 37, no. 1(2025), 141–176(Russian)) that, for every complete class X, there exists a nonnegative integer m with the following property: for every finite group G and each conjugacy class D of G, if every m elements of D generate a subgroup belonging to X, then ⟨D⟩ ∈ X. The smallest such m is called the Baer–Suzuki width of X denoted by BS(X). It is also proved(mod CFSG, ibid.) that, for a complete class X of symmetric boundary n, the value of BS(X) is at least n and is bounded above in terms of n. For every positive integer n ̸= 3, let f+ (n) and f− (n) be respectively the maximum and the minimum of BS(X), where X runs over all complete classes of symmetric boundary n. (a) Find f+ (n) for n = 4, 5, 6. It is known that f+ (1) = 2, f+ (2) = 3, and f+ (n) = 2(n − 1) for n ⩾ 7. (b) Is it true that f− (n) = n for all n ̸= 3? This is known to be true for n = 1, 2, 4.
target_in_paper: Problem 21.112(a)-(b) in the section New Problems (21st issue, 2026)
correct_elements: Your draft already reproduces the paper's official problem almost verbatim. In particular, it correctly states the definitions of a complete class, symmetric boundary, and Baer-Suzuki width BS(X); it correctly defines the extremal functions f_+(n) and f_-(n); and it preserves the two exact subquestions together with the known values f_+(1)=2, f_+(2)=3, f_+(n)=2(n-1) for n>=7, and the known cases f_-(n)=n for n=1,2,4.
missing_details: Make explicit that all groups under discussion are finite groups.
Define S_n as the symmetric group on n letters.
Define <D> as the subgroup generated by the conjugacy class D.
State explicitly that the symmetric boundary is defined only for a complete class X that is not the class of all finite groups.
Clarify that f_+(n) and f_-(n) are considered only for positive integers n!=3, since those are exactly the integers asserted in the problem statement to occur as symmetric boundaries.
For full stand-alone readability, restate the quantifiers in the definition of BS(X): the condition is required for every finite group G and every conjugacy class D of G.
refined_question: Let X be a nonempty class of finite groups that is closed under taking subgroups, homomorphic images, and extensions. For such a class X, assuming X is not the class of all finite groups, define its symmetric boundary to be the largest integer n for which the symmetric group S_n belongs to X. For each complete class X, let BS(X) denote the least nonnegative integer m with the following property: for every finite group G and every conjugacy class D of G, if every m elements of D generate a subgroup belonging to X, then the subgroup <D> generated by D also belongs to X. For each positive integer n!=3, define f_+(n)=max BS(X) and f_-(n)=min BS(X), where X ranges over all complete classes of finite groups with symmetric boundary n. Determine f_+(n) for n=4,5,6, given that f_+(1)=2, f_+(2)=3, and f_+(n)=2(n-1) for all n>=7; and decide whether f_-(n)=n for every positive integer n!=3, as is already known for n=1,2,4.
justification: The draft is already essentially the official formulation of Problem 21.112(a)-(b). The paper's actual intent is exactly to ask for the extremal Baer-Suzuki widths among complete classes of finite groups having a fixed symmetric boundary, with the specific unresolved cases f_+(4), f_+(5), f_+(6), and the general lower-extremal question whether f_-(n)=n for all admissible n. The only refinements needed are minor stand-alone clarifications of notation and quantifiers; no broader reformulation is warranted because the paper itself states precisely this two-part problem and does not provide a different equivalent version nearby.
